utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May we hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager. Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness is brought in, I said I had completed my examination-in-chief yesterday. I'm sorry, I forgot to ask one question. I wonder if I may reopen to ask one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence has no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness be brought in, please. In the meantime, for the transcript, I forgot yesterday to admit the following documents: S323 and S323-1. Hereby admitted into evidence. We discussed it already yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Merdzanic. You can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor has one or several additional questions. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Doctor, just, in fact, one question -- or maybe only one. I asked when you were walking down the street to the centre of Kozarac whether you had been able to see the mosque and you said no. Did you at any time, either on the journey from Prijedor to Trnopolje or thereafterwards when you left Trnopolje and went to Kozorac, did you see -- did you pass any of the mosques?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my way to Trnopolje, or rather from the camp, you could see a mosque. I did not pay much attention to mosques at that point. But even while we were in the camp still, that particular mosque was set fire to. And I heard later on that other mosques in the area were also burned down, but I did not see any of those myself, or at least I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The mosque that you saw on your way either to Trnopolje or from it, which one was that? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the mosque that was near the camp. You could, in fact, see it from the camp itself. I remember I saw that particular mosque. But right now, I can't visualise any of the other mosques I may have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The one you could see from the camp, do you know where that was, what area?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was roughly to the northwest of the camp. Perhaps 500 metres from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did the area have a name? Or was it part of Trnopolje itself?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each hamlet in that area had a name, but they were all part of Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry to press you on this, but are you able to say the name of the hamlet where the mosque was that you could see?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But on the sketch we used yesterday, perhaps I could point it out to you, the rough area where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you could have back, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The sketch you did of where Trnopolje was and the road to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp, the sketch of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. In that case, that is Exhibit 321-2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that mosque because later on we saw it burning. If you can please just blow this up a little bit so I can see the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we can't see anything at the moment. All right. But the witness needs to see the whole map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need the whole image. If you take this road towards Prijedor, I think the first street on the right led straight to the mosque. And the mosque was roughly in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to be given the map of the actual area of Prijedor that I think you looked at earlier and see if you can -- I can't remember what the number is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, that one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if perhaps you have another map, an even bigger one. The mosque may have been part of the hamlet of Trnjani. At any rate, it was in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry, Doctor. I won't press you further. I think that's the best we can probably achieve.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence is prepared for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the floor is yours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a good night's rest? We speak more or less the same language, so I would ask you to please pause a little after my question so that the interpreters could catch up and do their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try hard. If I speak too quickly, please, slow me down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no need to worry about that because both the Trial Chamber and the interpreters will be quick to warn us, I'm sure. My cross-examination will not take a particularly long time, and it will not be as strenuous as the examination-in-chief proved to be. I will merely just go through the transcript and ask you to clarify a number of points you said yesterday. As I go along, I'll mention the page numbers and line numbers. We are supposed to do this for the sake of the transcript, but you should not be confused by this. Can we begin, please. On page 7, line 21, you said that you worked in Trnopolje. Does this also refer to the period of April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that applies to that period of time, too, April and May 1992, until the moment I was detained in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You lived in Prijedor at that time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the attack on Kozarac, the conflict in Kozarac, what was the last time you were in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think at the health centre or in Kozarac, there should be some documents because we had our duty hours. And we had duty in Kozarac. And some of us did their duty in Prijedor. Those were night duties. Mine was in Kozarac. And on that particular occasion, I was on duty in Kozarac all through the night. And that's how I was stuck in Kozarac and could not leave Kozarac. I think that was immediately before the ultimatum. Prior to that, I could have left Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As there was a series of ultimatums, can you just clarify this, please: Was that the day just before the attack or the ultimatum of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no -- I have no knowledge of there being a whole series of ultimatums. I think this was two days before the attack, two days before the 24th, which means that the day we're talking about was probably the 22nd. I did not take part in the negotiations. I can't remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So two days before the attack, you arrived from Prijedor in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Two days before the attack is when people no longer had the possibility of leaving Kozarac which means that probably I had been in Kozarac for at least one day at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it normal, although you worked in Trnopolje, for you to be on duty in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was perfectly normal because in Trnopolje, there was no night duty. And all doctors in Kozarac did have to do night duties; and as Trnopolje was part of Kozarac, I did my duty -- I did my night duty in Kozarac. And those -- the other ones, they did their night duties in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to broach a different subject now. On page 9, line 14, the Prosecution asked you the following question: It was a question about the change in the relationship of Serbs, the attitude of the Serbs, towards the Muslims and Croats due to their failure to respond to the mobilisation callups, and also concerning the war in Croatia. You said that those who failed to respond to the callup were hunted done by the military police and that such people were taken forcibly to the front line and that Croats and Muslims often went into hiding because of that. Are you aware that there was an agreement that Muslims and Croats were not necessarily supposed to respond to the callup?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any such agreement, but I know a lot of persons who were hiding and who were even leaving Prijedor to go to distant places to hide. And I know that the MPs came knocking on people's doors to look for them to take them to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, to the best of your knowledge, how many were arrested in this way and sent to the front?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please provide us with one name of a person who had that sort of experience?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you the names of those persons who went into hiding. As far as those who were forced to go to the front, I can't give you a single name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 10, line 3, you speak about Serb soldiers returning from the front failing to return their weapons to the barracks, but rather, keeping their weapons. Do you know if there was an obligation for members of military units who returned from the front to hand their weapons back in?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I just know that they carried their weapons on them and they kept -- they kept those weapons in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 11, the last line on the page, you say that at the very beginning, it was possible to leave Kozarac and to pass through the checkpoints. You say there were checkpoints not only around Kozarac but also in Orlovci, as well as along the Trnopolje/Prijedor Road. You go on to claim that after the expiry of the ultimatum for Kozarac, Muslims were from that moment on no longer allowed to leave Kozarac. During your visits to Kozarac from Prijedor, did you see any checkpoints set up and controlled by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen a single Bosniak-controlled checkpoint, nor was I ever searched at any such checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that you did not see the checkpoint in Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see a checkpoint in Kozarusa. Whose checkpoint did you have in mind, Serb-held or Bosniak-held checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bosniak-held checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen -- I've seen neither. Can you tell me exactly where Kozarusa is?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the village just before Kozarac on the Prijedor/Kozarac Road if you travel from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw a checkpoint there, a checkpoint with soldiers looking at people's documents or stopping vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see a Bosnian-held checkpoint in Kozarac itself, about 200 metres off the main road?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A checkpoint, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time in Kozarac, did you see any armed persons? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime before the ultimatum expired and in the two days before the shelling, yes. You could see here and there perhaps a uniformed, armed person. Sometimes you could perhaps see a civilian walking around carrying a weapon. And as I've pointed out before, I went to see Cirkin; and when I came there, I saw a group of young men who were carrying weapons. It was not a very large group. I can't say if others were somewhere else. But when I came there, there were, perhaps, about 15 young men with uniforms and weapons there. I have to add, however, that I did not spend that much time just walking about Kozarac. I was there to work, and perhaps I could see a thing or two on my way to work or whenever we went to the pharmacy to get the medicines for the clinic. But normally, I did not get to move about that much. Prior to that, however, I did go from Kozarac to Trnopolje to the clinic. I went to work in an ambulance. And I know that to the left of the road, there was a JNA tank; and to the right, there was a bus stop. And JNA soldiers were standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long before the clash in Kozarac did you see that tank?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact number of days, but I think from the moment the JNA took over Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Kozarac, did you learn of the existence of any armed groups such as Ramiz's group or Kola's group?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz's group is unfamiliar to me. I heard about Kola from other people's stories. People told me that there was a man named Kola, but I couldn't give you any further details on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 13, line 11, again, you refer to the moment the ultimatum expired. You say that people were no longer allowed to leave Kozarac. Was there any such order not allowing people to leave Kozarac, or were people just simply afraid to leave? What was it that kept people from leaving?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders by which side?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to please clarify this point for us, why people no longer left Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at the Orlovci checkpoint, people were often turned back. Their IDs would be checked there, and they would be turned back to Kozarac. So this is how they returned to Kozarac and were actually not able to leave the town. This is what my patients told me, including the two pregnant women whose babies I delivered. This is just a piece of information that I heard from others. Whether there was any such order, I don't know. Well, I am sure that there were people who were simply afraid to even try and leave Prijedor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, were any entries into Kozarac allowed? Were other people allowed entry into Kozarac from the outside?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't affirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 22 -- I apologise. Just a moment. On page 24, in line 3, you spoke about the second location of the clinic at the outskirts of Kozarac. You told us that it was a house which was naturally protected by a small hill and wood. You also told us that in that house, there were members of the police force in that house, the police who had already moved in. In those days, do you know how many people -- how many members of the Kozarac -- how many days prior to that had those members of the police force been relocated to that house?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 25, line 19, you speak about how you were trying to get a permission to transport the wounded children outside Kozarac. You also told us that this was not allowed to you, that you never got that permission, and you also mentioned the fact that you had spoken to someone for that purpose. Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know who the individual was. He never introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, after the surrender, it was the wounded who left the Kozarac first at the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The wounded left the town first. They were followed by the police, and finally by the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You made mention of a dead man who remained at the clinic. You also told us that later on, you went back to the clinic but that you did not find him. Do you know who it was who removed his body from the clinic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may have been members of his family, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 27, you speak about the killings that occurred in the Sahoric house. You stated that people had been killed by a hand-held rocket launcher. In Trnopolje, did you have an opportunity to talk to the people who had participated in the burial of these men?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I don't know what happened afterwards. This woman went to see Major Kuruzovic, but I don't know what happened later. I don't know whether this woman is still alive, but I know that she was living in Germany for a while. And I still have her phone number and the phone number of her son. So I think that one could find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did she ever mention to you the fact that some of the people in this group had been armed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which group?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, she didn't say anything -- she didn't say anything specific. She just mentioned this long-barrelled weapon which was used to fire a rocket and which was hand-held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you knew that other witnesses in this case had claimed that these people had been killed by an automatic weapon, would you be prepared to accept that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I was not there. I was not present when this incident took place. I just told you the story of an eyewitness of this woman who told me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 34, you speak about your arrival in the Trnopolje camp. You say that everything was disorganised, that there was no food provided. Is it your impression that the decision to accommodate people there had been taken in a hasty manner, or did you feel that it had all been planned in advance?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say. Both are possible actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked in Trnopolje for a while. Are you aware of the fact that Serb refugees from Bosanska Bojna had been accommodated in Trnopolje prior to the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serb refugees from Croatia in Trnopolje in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that. I didn't treat in my clinic any of these refugees at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you never heard from other people who visited your clinic there that there was a large number of Serb refugees from Croatia and Bosanska Bojna living in Trnopolje at the time?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 69, you spoke about the fact that Serbs had ethnically cleansed village by village. When you were in Trnopolje, you were not able to know where exactly and in which villages the fighting took place?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're quite right. We didn't know about the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the following page, page 70, you told us that whenever Serbs entered a village, they had with them lists with the names of the people that were to be killed. Did you personally ever see any such list?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that sometimes they would come to the camp with such lists. I know that Slavko Puhalic used one of such lists to find Vasif Gutic's relatives. I don't know whether those were the same lists, but I simply told you what I had heard from the refugees of these villages, that is, that they had searched for people according to some lists with names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of function did Slavko Puhalic have in the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was Slobodan Kuruzovic's deputy. He was not a simple guard at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what rank he held?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he walked around without any particular insignia of rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did he wear?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, he wore a green and brown camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that Slavko Puhalic had told you at one point in time that a meeting was supposed to be held where a decision to the effect that only 3 per cent of the Muslim population should be allowed to stay in Prijedor was supposed to be reached. Can you tell us when it was that Slavko Puhalic told you this?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been sometime in July, but I couldn't tell you exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else present when you talked, when the two of you talked?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this conversation took place at the clinic, so other people may have been present. I don't think actually that we were alone. Azra was maybe present, or Dr. Gutic. I don't know. But we were not alone definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "Gutic," "Dr. Gutic," you mean Vasif Gutic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vasif Gutic, medical student. He was not a doctor yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have an open conversation with Slavko Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What exactly do you have in mind when you say "an open conversation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you friends with Slavko Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not friends. I mean, we didn't know each other from before. We never socialised; we were never friends, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 72, you speak about a convoy which was organised in Trnopolje and which eventually left for Mount Vlasic. You told us that anyone could join this convoy and that it was not organised on the basis of any lists. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Finish your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any women and children join this particular convoy?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, women and children also joined this convoy. I just wanted to add that normally there were no lists made for any convoys, not on that occasion nor before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 74, when asked by the Prosecutor as to any preparations that may have been done before the visit of the journalists, you said that there had been a fence set up before their arrival fencing off one portion of the camp where detainees who had arrived from Omarska and Keraterm were placed. I should like to know how many days prior to the visit of the journalists this fence had been put up, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days maybe. Right before the visit of the journalists, at any rate. It had not been there for any longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it was taken off before the second visit of the journalists?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So how long was it in place, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten days, maybe two weeks at the maximum. One can easily calculate the date of the second visit of the journalists because when they arrived for the second time, it was no longer there. At any rate, it was there for a brief period of time only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, it was fencing off the area where people who had been brought from Omarska and Keraterm were placed; no other detainees were there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, at the time when the fence was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later, when the fence was taken down, the people from Omarska and Keraterm mingled with other detainees in Keraterm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's -- the question was one you wanted to state, in Trnopolje, and not in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a mistake in the transcript, so let me ask my question once again, although you have already given your answer. I may have phrased it wrongly. Speaking of the people from Omarska and Keraterm, were they later together with other detainees of Trnopolje after the fence had been taken down?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They were together with other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Major Kuruzovic have a house with an office in the vicinity of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a house very close to Trnopolje. I can show you exactly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where it was on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who stayed in this house?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly. He constantly moved around with the Balaban brothers. Slavko Puhalic was also there very often. As to who stayed with him in this house, I don't know. I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please provide the witness with the sketch of Trnopolje. I don't recall the exact exhibit number. I think it was -1 or -2, please. Can you point out on this sketch where the house was located you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here were the quarters of Major Kuruzovic. At the very beginning of the camp's operation, I'm not sure if he was there or somewhere else. But I know for sure that at a later stage, he was spending all of his time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, we are discussing now on the basis of -- Madam Registrar, could you please give me the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: S321-2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the basis of S321-2, on the top of this sketch to the right-hand side. Did you want to indicate the first or the second house to be seen on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This house with the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be to the right-hand side on the top of this sketch. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how you learned that Major Kuruzovic was staying in that house? Could you actually see the house? Did you pass the house?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the sketch is no longer at hand. I used to pass by a house that was closer to where I was staying. But I saw the other house there, and I was told that Major Kuruzovic was staying in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll show you the sketch again so you can show us everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to pass this house. There were two women here, two women I was supposed to examine. And here, there was a guard post. From Kozarac, you could see this area here. And it was no secret, after all. Everyone knew that Major Kuruzovic was staying in that particular house. I had no need to pass that particular house to know that he was staying there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, the witness pointed to a house located on the road, to the left-hand side of the road, on the top of the sketch, the second house on the left-hand side. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that house, aside from Major Kuruzovic, were there any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a guard post right here. As to whether there were any soldiers actually staying in Major Kuruzovic's house, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilians staying in that house?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. Those houses were empty. It was only in this house here that those two women were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Major Kuruzovic's house, were any detainees being kept there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I knew. I never went to that house, so I was not in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke about convoys, and we said that no lists were being drawn up for the convoys. However, on page 81, you also mentioned that you were forced to sign certain documents without which no person was allowed to leave the camp. Do you know if those documents had been issued by people from the Red Cross? Were those documents signed by Pero Curguz?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those documents were not signed by Pero Curguz. Those were uniformed persons. We didn't know who they were; they weren't guards. But this only applies to the very last convoy when the camp was being closed down and when I was on my way out. That was the only convoy for which the signing of those documents was required. That was the convoy with the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the obligation to sign over property, to sign over your property to Republika Srpska, was that document signed by anyone from the Serb authorities or from the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Certainly no one from the International Red Cross. We did speak to the International Red Cross and asked them what we should do. What they told us was: "Just go ahead and sign those documents because no laws will acknowledge such documents, and you can sign it without worrying because those documents would not be used." We had benches put in front of us, and one by one we had to sign those documents. And only after each one of us had signed those documents were we allowed to get on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Aside from the last convoy which you joined and which was organised by the International Red Cross, do you know who had organised the previous convoys?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous convoys had been organised by the Serbs. Kuruzovic would always know about convoys at least a day ahead. And then apart from the guards, there would usually be some military personnel there. There was this man Branko Beric. I think he was a veterinarian technician. With a number of his own people, they would just line up on either side of the road, and then women and children two by two would join the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that actually those convoys had been organised by the Republika Srpska Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a Red Cross office had been opened in Trnopolje as early as the 28th or 29th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An office of the Serbian Red Cross was opened -- I can't remember the exact date. But I agree that it was in late May that they arrived in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw yesterday that in Trnopolje, you had a camera in your possession. Was the camera yours or did it belong to Azra Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It belonged -- the camera belonged to Azra Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you searched on your way into the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not searched upon our arrival in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have your personal documents on you?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had my ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 82, line 13, you said what happened in the old town in Prijedor had nothing to do with the war. You went on to explain that the destruction, the burning of that district of Prijedor, was a result completely unrelated to any military activities.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which side members of Bosniak and Croat units had arrived from during the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the attack when we left the camp. I heard something about the attack even during my stay in the camp. I heard that they passed through those parts, but the houses were bulldozed into the ground long after those activities, long after the military activities in Prijedor had ceased. Kozarac itself was not destroyed during the shelling. But after everyone had already been expelled, that's when they pulled down all the churches and mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know about another attack on Kozarac and another attempt by Bosnian forces led by Alagic, Kemal, also known as Divjak, to take Kozarac back?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the fiercest fighting on the 30th of May, 1992, that is, did you hear about this from the other people with whom you were staying in Trnopolje, that the fiercest fighting took place in the old town and on Partizanska Street?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about one single attack on Prijedor. I couldn't tell you the date, but what I heard was that everyone was captured or killed within a single day. We also heard that one of the Serbs there got killed on that day. I can't remember that person's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that within the framework of the Kozarac Territorial Defence there was also a medical corps?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. What I did know is that afterwards, they asked us where all the surgeons from Croatia were, that apparently there was a bunker hospital somewhere, that all the surgery equipment was buried underground somewhere. But all those obviously were lies and fabrications.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 83, line 10, you say you were approached by Mladen Mitrovic. Allegedly he had orders to kill you and to keep you from leaving the camp alive. Did Mladen Mitrovic tell you on that occasion who he had received that order from?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me. And I'm not sure whether he was just out to intimidate me or whether he really meant what he said. Speaking of which, I forgot to say that Mladen Mitrovic had taken five people out of the camp and killed them, unregistered people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last incident you have just described, was that also a result of an order, or was it Mladen Mitrovic acting of his accord?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this: The military or the military police, I think they had white belts, they arrived in a military vehicle from Prijedor with five people, and these five persons were then handed over to the guard in Trnopolje. They put them up in the local commune building. After that, a man wearing a military uniform arrived in a civilian vehicle and entered that room with Mladen Mitrovic. They beat those people for a very long time, and then they took them outside the building one by one towards the pond. And they kept beating them on their way to the pond, and eventually killed those people down there. That's what we heard. I'm not sure, but we heard that Major Kuruzovic was fishing at the pond at that time, and that he had actually made the decision to have those people killed because they had not been registered up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were all the other people in Trnopolje registered?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time already. But there were three registered persons who were taken to Kozarac for forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the video footage made by Penny Marshall about the inmates of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I did, yes. Whether there was more, I don't know. But I certainly did see some of her footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was shown before the Court here, so we don't want to waste time on this now. But let me just ask you the following question: Penny Marshall went into the fenced-off area of the construction material shop that was fenced off with barbed-wire, and she was taking footage of people inside the camp -- inside the fencing, the barbed-wire fencing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Let me explain this to you. When Penny Marshall came, the inmates from Keraterm had already been brought there. If you show me sketch number 2, perhaps I can explain everything to you. It's a sketch just like this one, but a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Sketch number 2 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the one. The first time Penny Marshall came, the inmates from Keraterm were here. And the fencing stretched from the big hall, and then this stretch of the fencing had been there before. This is the fence next to the shop. And then a fence was put up here, and the inmates she filmed were inside this area here which was fenced off. She came in through the fence, and she was inside the fencing surrounding the shop. At that time, the large convoy from Omarska which was later put here had not arrived. So she was filming from this fenced-off area -- she was filming a different fenced-off area. I'm not sure if the Prosecutor has those films, but I have pictures showing exactly the positions of those inmates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I please ask the witness to mark on the document before you the exact position of this fence you mentioned. And then let us take this document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sketch here, I marked it as number 3. It's the dotted line here. Here is where the hall was, and then a fence was put up here. This fence had been there already. And this fence was then made for the inmates from Keraterm. So it was completely fenced off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You have a marker in your hand. Could you please mark this line once again with the marker. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the fence that had been put Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. up at some time -- some time earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your testimony today is that in addition to the fence facing the person filming on that video footage, we should also be able to see the lateral fencing.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that I saw a tape in which, yes, you can see. I was at a trial in London, and we were talking about that particular fence. We had video footage showing fencing from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The lateral fence you've just mentioned, how high was it, can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean this one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fence on the side, well, the highest part of the fencing, the one that belonged to the fence, was over 2 metres high. And the one I'm talking about may have been about a metre and a half. I think the one on the other side was even lower, perhaps up to my chest, but certainly not 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This fencing stretched all the way to the dom building, the community centre building?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It surrounded the community centre, and then the right-hand stretch of this fencing and the fencing surrounding the shop, that was a closed circle, the fencing, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain then how the women and children entered the community centre, the dom, if the gate was made of wire?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain this. Women and children were not in the cultural centre at all. Before the journalists came, there was a convoy which the women and children joined and left the camp. Some of the men left with that convoy, too. The remaining women were put up on one of the upper floors where the offices of the football club used to be, and then there was a flight of stairs on the outside of the building which you could see to reach the upper floor. And then the camp inmates from Keraterm, who had arrived from Keraterm, they could enter this hall here. And in this hall, there were just male inmates and no women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the camp inmates, the male camp inmates, allowed to enter the community centre?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were allowed to enter the big hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the women and children? Where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the upper floor where the offices of the local football club used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] It would be a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Before the break, could the witness please mark with the marker he has in his hands all the areas where there were fences, and please indicate those fences that were, according to your testimony, pulled down for the one or other purpose so that we are aware where there was normally a fence in addition to that what you marked already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fence made specially before the arrival of the inmates from Keraterm that is this stretch here, this stretch here, and this stretch here. The fence that had already existed went all the way around. I think it had a hole here, and another hole there. Afterwards both these fences were taken down, both of them. This part of the fencing here, the construction material shop, it was also a wire fence. But the poles were made of steel. And this fence here made by the inmates had wooden poles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So could you please, because it's difficult to understand from the transcript, mark especially the part of the fence that was pulled down sometimes by crossing this part of the fence. And then additionally, also with a marker, mark the other parts of the fence. But first, the part of the fence which was sometimes pulled down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't quite understand, Your Honour. What do you mean by "sometimes pulled down"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- you just pointed to this area that for the purposes of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation I got was "fence taken down." So I didn't quite get the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that on several occasions, a fence was pulled down. And could you please indicate the distinction between what one could call a permanent fence and a provisional fence. You made, just some minutes before, the distinction yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. The fence that had been there, that's this fence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a dotted line representing that fence. Dot line, dot line, dot line. That's how I marked it on my drawing. Every fence is marked in a different way. Dot line, dot line. So this is the fence that had been there from before. The fence that was made immediately before the arrival of the inmates just has lines and no dots.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion, that be marked in one colour and the other in another. It may become a little bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have for the other one, yes. Blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, once again, what you are marking now additional in blue. That's which fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I circled this in blue now. That's the fence that was put up immediately before the arrival of the camp inmates from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any additional? We can see a little bit higher on the same sketch also such a line. Does this mean that there was also a kind of fence? This one, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this one here surrounding the school building. That's also another fence that had been there earlier. It was a very small, low iron fence. There was another very low fence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you mark it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Outside the clinic courtyard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Those fences you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the gate. I think it stretched up to here somewhere. And then the school building fence here, there was a gate, and here there was a fence surrounding the school building. There was another gate here, I think, through which you could pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any additional remarks to this sketch by the parties, or questions? This is not the case. Then this document previously marked as S324 will be with the additional marks on it now Exhibit Number S324-1. And may we please ask the Office of the Prosecutor to provide the parties and the Bench with colour copies of S324-1, and the registry, please, not to be forgotten. The trial stays adjourned until 11.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And the Defence may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Merdzanic, I should like to show you a video footage, and then later on ask you if you can clarify for us which fence exactly we are talking about. I think that some of the fences will be visible on the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Say it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you need to make a comment, Doctor, please, let us know and we will stop the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But first of all, let's start the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This here is the fence connecting the big hall, and this section here. This is the fence I was talking about, the one on the side which is connecting the large hall and the fence which is separating the area of the construction material shop. Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, conclude that the fence was about waist high, or slightly higher, 10 centimetres or so?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the height of the person, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that it was not made of barbed-wire but of mesh wire?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we continue now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. This fence here that we see in front of us is the fence of the shop, I think. And the one leading further on is the one fencing off the road. But I think we will see it in a minute. Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we stop here --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification. This is correct, that we can see a barbed-wire fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the fence which you can see here on the south side of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this fence in place before surrounding the area much the construction material shop?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was there before. You also have footage showing Penny Marshall -- I don't think you can see it here, but you can see it on the other footage, the moment that she entered the area on this particular spot here. Perhaps we will see it later on this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can we proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, I'm sorry, because of the lack of time we have a number of different versions of this film, unfortunately. I looked at one which does show the fence, I think, that the doctor is talking about. It is bad quality. This one I don't think is going to help. The video technicians have in the booth another video which has been set up in the right place. It's 0910. I wonder if that can be inserted and we will see, I think, what the doctor is thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But first of all, Defence should --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, the Defence should have the chance to continue on the basis of their contribution. Do you want to make any additional comments to the video we are playing right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously that it's not easy to work with this video, so we will move on and try to clarify and to ask questions about some photographs. And if we find better video, maybe it would be possible to clarify some other questions regarding the fences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you agree that we continue with the video ready for being played right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it's possible to work on that video, based on that video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if Mr. Lukic doesn't mind, it may help him and the doctor if we just try and insert the other video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, let's work on the basis of the other video. Could it be played right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we rewind a little bit, please. Stop. Stop. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. This is the fence alongside the road, this one here. These are the soldiers standing on the road. This fence is not the one surrounding the construction material shop, but the one leading further above. What we're still lacking is the photograph of the area above, but I haven't seen an image of that area. I don't think it can be found. So we have three sides of this fenced-in area established. But as for the fourth side of the area, I don't think I've ever seen a video or a photograph showing that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we just, for clarification, ask for rewinding to the beginning of this clip, that you may comment on this. Please rewind to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is probably -- it is a close-up, but we can see that this is the same kind of the fence as the one we saw a moment ago but which was not -- it did not have the added -- don't have barbed-wire added to it, the one alongside the road. It did not have the barbed-wire added on top of it. But I don't think that it makes any significant difference. The fence was made of the material that was available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for this fence where we can see barbed wire, is this a part of the fence which had been in place and which surrounded the construction material shop on the south side?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see right now, yes, I think that this is the one on the south side of the area. But the one that we saw a moment ago with those soldiers standing on the road, you will see it -- you can see it -- I think it has the same barbed wire on top of it. We can have a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please play the video again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's gone now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. And rewind a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop and rewind a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please. I think that this is the fence. These are the soldiers standing on the road, and this is the fence going alongside the road. You can see that there is a barbed wire on top of it. But I don't think it's very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Bench wants to leave it to the parties to provide us with the necessary stills if they regard it necessary for the purpose of evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour. So we won't be needing this video any more. Thank you. I would like the usher to present to the witness S321-4, please. 6 and 7. Would you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that the man who is lying next to this paramedic is one of the patients, one of the inmates.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. He spent one night at the clinic. I think that this was early on immediately after our arrival in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you the following: On this photograph, we see that the man is shaven.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which man do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The patient.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can see is that his hand is on his face, so I cannot really tell whether he's neatly shaven or not. At least not on the basis of this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see the part of the face where the moustache is?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how old this person is. I am sure that it was a very young man. I'm not even sure whether he had already started shaving at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. S321-6, please. On this photograph we see the lady whom you called Babica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the upper photograph is showing Babica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that she is covered with a blanket.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, with a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] May we see now S321-7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When taking these photographs, did you use a flash? At least, this is the impression we get by watching this photograph.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that we used a flash, yes. Azra should know whether this camera has a flash or not. But it is possible that we used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you told us that you took these photographs secretly. Is it possible for him not to have noticed your taking a photograph of him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is. He was in a very bad shape. His eyes were so swollen that he couldn't see anything almost. If you have a closer look at his mouth and his nose, you will see how swollen they are. This man obviously didn't know where he was. He was half conscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, therefore, that when taking photographs of your patients with a flash, you didn't think that they would know that they were being filmed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not sure, of course, but it was our assumption that they would not notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] May we now see S321-14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This man here, you said that he had spent a long time in Trnopolje. Do you know what his name was?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know his name. But I think he was from the village of Trnjani, from that area. When you go from Trnopolje to Prijedor, the village of Hrnici, I think there's a village there called Hrnici along the road leading from Trnopolje to, well, yeah, I think it's the village of Hrnici. If I could just have a map to have another look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him about his name when you examined him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I even know we knew his name, but I did not memorise it. There may be other witnesses who do remember, but those people who were with me there certainly know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] May we now see S15-15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this group of people had arrived from Keraterm or Omarska, or were these people inmates at Trnopolje also?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man in the forefront is one of the persons who had been transferred from Keraterm or Omarska. I don't know him. I didn't see him there. As for the others, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please try to remember if this photograph was taken when the persons from Keraterm and Omarska were being kept apart from everyone else in Trnopolje, or can you not remember?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photo was taken later, after the arrival of the journalists when the fence had been taken down and when other journalists and photographers began to arrive and take pictures. So this was definitely taken by a journalist. This photograph was not taken by one of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's quite obvious, if you look at the photo, that aside from this man in the foreground here who looks emaciated, all the other people in the background look regularly or well-fed. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do agree. But if you remember the video where you can see the people behind the fence, you will probably agree with me that those people look severely underfed, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, I hereby conclude my cross-examination. I thank you sincerely for answering our questions. I wish you a safe trip back to wherever you live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the Prosecution, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's limited what we have as questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you, I know you mentioned this earlier, when you stayed in Trnopolje, was the camp ever visited by high-ranking military persons or high-ranking politicians, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to make this distinction. High-ranking military personnel or politicians from where and which party soever.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a military delegation came with a high-ranking officer. I don't know what his name was. That was a group of Serb officers. There was another man with them wearing plainclothes. He was not from ex-Yugoslavia at all. I can't remember now. He was an important politician or a delegate. He was quite tall. And he was accompanied by a lady translator, interpreter. I can't remember his name. I think that was the highest ranking and most influential delegation to have arrived in Trnopolje. There were a number of journalists later on who came and went. But I think that military delegation with high-ranking officers and an officer who may have been an American officer or a representative of the United Nations; I can't tell you who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could you tell us, was it in the beginning or in the middle or by the end of the period of time you had to stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was quite certainly after the visit of the journalists. I don't know if the International Red Cross had already arrived or not. But it may have been at some point in August, perhaps mid-August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And to be on the safe side, I previously asked for high-ranking military personnel or politicians. Was there ever any other delegation or a visit by other military personnel or politicians in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only talk about the clinic, so it was that delegation that I've already referred to. I think on one occasion, a human rights expert, an American, I think came too. I believe there was another delegation visiting the camp, but they didn't visit the clinic. I can no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now turn to another issue. I didn't understand what you told us this morning. It may be my mistake, on page 21, line 4. You said: "I heard about the attack. When we left the camp, I heard something about the attack even during my stay in the camp. I heard that they passed through those parts, but the houses were bulldozed into the ground long after those activities, long after the military activities in Prijedor had ceased. Kozarac itself was not destroyed during the shelling, but after everyone had already been expelled. That's when they pulled down all the churches and mosques." Could you please try to make a distinction, to the best of your recollection, what did you -- in what condition did you see Kozarac the last time you yourself had seen Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw our clinic. Its walls were shell pimpled, and the windows were shattered. And the roof was burned through by a shell. So that was the type of damage we had. After I left the camp, I saw pictures of Kozarac that were taken at a later stage. And you could see the whole street leading from the junction outside Kozarac, I saw buildings in those photographs completely destroyed which was not the case when we were leaving Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So to be quite clear, you saw Kozarac, the buildings, destroyed in part, and then later on, for what purposes soever, it was bulldozed down that there was no reminder. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they used bulldozers or if Kozarac was mined, but I know that in the old town they did indeed use bulldozers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And once again, the same question with respect to the old town. Is it correct that first the old town was destroyed and houses there were destroyed in the same manner as you just mentioned as with respect to Kozarac, and then later on everything was, yeah, be it bulldozed or in what way soever prepared that there could be seen no reminder of this part of Prijedor? Would this be correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct. As far as I know, the attack on Prijedor, they just passed through, and the clashes took place in the town itself. So in the old town, there wasn't nearly as much damage as in Kozarac during the shelling. And the attack finished. Those young men were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. captured or killed. And in the old town, the houses were completely preserved with civilians still living inside those houses. I'm telling you all this because my sister's husband was still staying there. And then they were all taken away and taken to the camps. After the houses had been looted, I had some construction materials in my house, for example, and they took those things away in lorries. So whatever they couldn't destroy by bulldozing, they simply burned the foundations of those houses, but that was quite a while after the original attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see the old town personally after the attack?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is based on that what you heard from neighbours and relatives. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we, for a moment, go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On the video we could see today, we could see one guard in civilian clothes. In this regard, I would like to ask you: Who ran the camp? Militaries? Paramilitaries? Police? Or whosoever?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Kuruzovic, at least as far as I knew, was in charge of the camp. And he would come to the camp wearing military uniform. Before the war, he was a civilian. He was not an active military officer. They called him "Major" which means that he probably had the rank of major. He was always wearing a uniform. But before the war, I repeat, he was not an active military officer. I think he was a teacher, a primary school teacher, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what about the rest of the camp personnel, who they were?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all wearing military uniform. The only exception was Dr. Dusko Ivic and Mica. Sometimes they wore a military uniform, but sometimes they would just come in wearing plainclothes. The Serbian Red Cross, they were also wearing plainclothes, not military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, the Major Kuruzovic and other military personnel, whom they were subordinated to, the authorities in Prijedor or the authorities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about their hierarchy, how it was organised, the chain of command. It must have gone through Prijedor, and then Prijedor probably cooperated with the higher levels. But this is merely my own opinion. Perhaps they were in touch. Probably they weren't in touch directly with Karadzic. Probably first they went to Prijedor, and then from Prijedor on to the higher levels of decision-making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Hvala, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's only one thing that arises out of Your Honours' questions that's really this. We do have a video of Kozarac - I think it was played in opening - taken in November 1992. I don't know whether before the witness leaves, Your Honour would like him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be an excellent idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honour wants to adjourn now for the break. We need to hunt it down. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness shouldn't be waiting for such a long period. If we could start now, I have one additional question. Maybe the Defence does as well. If Mr. Koumjian could come immediately, this would be excellent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ought to because I think I played it in opening. If somebody can just find the tape that I played in opening. I don't know whether it went to the Court after that. No. All right, we are doing a search at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I, in addition, ask you, no doubt, it's for the Judges to decide finally on the criminal responsibility of individuals. But nevertheless, no doubt, you yourself have, when recalling all these incidents happening in the area of Prijedor, Kozarac, Trnopolje, what is your personal view? Who is responsible from your point of view for that what happened in the area in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was planned years ahead. Most probably the planning by the Serbs started with Milosevic, and those plans must have been revamped when the disintegration of Yugoslavia began, when the war broke out, when clashes started breaking out. I think top-level Serb politicians were war-mongering and using propaganda to persuade their people to oppose the Muslims and Croats. It took some persuasion to convince my Serb neighbour with whom I had lived my whole life that I was suddenly his enemy and that I was to be killed. I don't understand how else this could be done. I must say that there were Serbs who helped us, those who could. But they were forced to take up arms and to fight alongside with the other Serbs because they could either join them or oppose them. There was no middle ground. I remember an elderly man who came to work as a guard at the Trnopolje camp. He was an acquaintance of Mujo Tehnicar. He came to our clinic. He was crying. He asked, he said if there was anything I could do to help you, I would give you weapons, ammunition, anything. But there was nothing much he could do, he said. I think Serb propaganda was very strong. They said that Muslims were preparing attacks against Serb civilians and children. They talked about lists being drawn up. So allegedly, they were arming their own people for the defence against Muslims. So probably the true skill of their politicians was the way they managed to persuade their own people to wage war on others. I think the greatest responsibility rests with the top levels of decision-making among the Serb politicians. There were many Serbs probably who even failed to notice how they had been drawn into that. Take, for example, the following issue: Why was I put into the camp and then held there for such a long time? What did I do? Can they name at least one thing that I did wrong? Mr. Stakic is here. He's a physician just like I am, and he made decisions concerning the camps. He knew that we were there. He knew that his colleague Jusuf Pasic, who was facing retirement, had been taken to Omarska and killed there. He knew about dozens of doctors, physicians being taken to Omarska and killed. Why? What for? Why were those people killed? Those people were the Muslim intelligencia, and they meant something, they were prominent people. Is there an answer to all of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you for these very personal remarks. May I ask the parties, are there any further questions emanating from this line of questions put by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would like to have the power to object every time when you pose this question, Your Honour. But as we don't have that kind of power, we don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said earlier in this case, we have to make a clear distinction between the criminal responsibility, but it is also of extreme value to hear the opinions based on own experience, yes, on experience at that time in the area that we get a view. And no doubt, it's, as I mentioned, a very personal view.
